The Indian Space Research Organisation, ISRO, is India's national space agency, founded in 1969 and based in Bengaluru. It grew out of a committee set up in 1962 by the physicist Vikram Sarabhai, who argued that a poor country needed satellites for weather, phones and teaching, not for prestige.

Early rockets were carried to the launch site on bicycles and bullock carts. The first Indian satellite, Aryabhata, went up on a Soviet rocket in 1975, eighteen years after Sputnik 1. India launched its own satellite on its own rocket in 1980.

ISRO became known for doing a lot with little money:

  • Communication and weather satellites that serve TV, phones and cyclone warnings.
  • The Mars Orbiter Mission, which reached Mars on the first try in 2014.
  • Chandrayaan-3, which landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023.

Most launches fly from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota.
